title: Let's: suggestions and wishes
intro: This unit is about wanting things to happen. The optative says **let me** and **let's**: *Kömek edeýinmi?*, shall I help?; *Gideli!*, let's go! The third-person form in `-sYn` says **let him**, **let them**: *Ol gelsin*, let him come. The same `-sYn` is in every good wish: *bolsun*, may it be, as in *Toýuňyz gutly bolsun!*, congratulations on your celebration. And *bolýar*, which you know as **OK**, also asks and refuses: *Bolýarmy?*, *Bolmaz!*

blocks.text: You already have the commands for **you**: *Gel!*, *Geliň!* ([A1 unit 12](a1-u12)). For **me** and **us** Turkmen has the optative. It offers, proposes and suggests: **let me**, **I'll**, **shall I?**, **let's**, **shall we?**

The first vowel of the ending follows the stem: *e* after front vowels, *a* after back ones. A stem ending in a vowel just adds *-ýyn*, *-ly* or *-lyň*: *oka-* → *okaýyn*, *okaly*. A final *e* becomes *ä*, as before *-p* and *-r*: *işle-* → *işläýin*, *işläli*. And the *t*-verbs voice their *t*, since the ending starts with a vowel: *gideýin*, *edeýin*, *aýdaýyn*.

rows.en: let me go, I'll go, I'll be off

blocks.text: **Two or more.** `-AlY` is for two people, you and me; with `-AlYň` you speak to a group, three or more. Often the command *Gel!* or *Geliň!* comes first, like English **come on**: *Gel, gideli!* to one friend; *Geliň, başlalyň!* to everyone in the room.

**Questions** take `-mY` as usual, written on: *Kömek edeýinmi?*, shall I help?; *Gapyny açaýynmy?*, shall I open the door?; *Gidelimi?*, shall we go? The question is how you offer to do something for someone, and how you propose a plan.

blocks.title: *gitmek*: shall I go? shall we go?

blocks.text: **Negative.** `-mA` goes before the ending, and its *e* becomes *ä*: *gitmäýin*, let me not go; *gitmäli*, *gitmäliň*, let's not go. You will meet these less often, and with back vowels the plural looks just like **must**: *almaly* can be **let's not take** or **must take**. To turn down a plan, the usual way is with *bolýar* (the last section).

blocks.title: *gitmek*: let me not go, let's not go

items.en: Let me bring you some tea.

blocks.title: Not the future
blocks.text: *Men gideýin* is an offer or a decision made now: **I'll be off, let me go**. A plan is `-jAk` or `-ýAr`: *Men ertir gitjek*. And the optative takes no other ending: `gideýinim` and `gidelik` are not forms.

For **him, her, it** and **them**, add `-sYn` to the stem: *gel-* → *gelsin*, let him come; *otur-* → *otursyn*, let her sit down. The plural adds *-lAr*: *gelsinler*, *otursynlar*. The vowel follows harmony, and after a rounded first syllable it rounds, as you learned in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *bolsun*, *görsün*.

blocks.title: *gelmek*: let him come, let them come

rows.en: let him, her or it come

blocks.text: Since `-sYn` starts with a consonant, stems don't change: *gitsin*, *etsin*, *işlesin*. **Negative**: `-mA` before it, *gelmesin*, let him not come, he shouldn't come. **Question**: *gelsinmi?*, should he come? shall I tell him to come?

rows.en: let him not come; he shouldn't come

blocks.text: Use it to pass on what someone should do, to give permission, and to say what you want to happen: *Merdan içeri girsin*, Merdan can come in; *Çagalar oýnasynlar*, let the children play; *Ol maňa jaň etsin*, tell her to call me.

blocks.title: English let
blocks.text: English uses one word, **let**, for three things Turkmen keeps apart: **let me** (*geleýin*), **let's** (*geleli*) and **let him** (*gelsin*). Choose by who will do it.

*bolsun* is `-sYn` on *bolmak*: **may it be**. Most Turkmen good wishes are built on it: the thing you wish well, with **your**, then how you wish it to be, then *bolsun*. *Toýuňyz gutly bolsun!*, literally **may your celebration be blessed**, congratulations. The possessive follows the person: *-ň* to one friend, *-ňYz* politely or to several.

blocks.text: *gutly* means **blessed, festive**; *rowaç* is **going well, prospering**; *işdä* is **appetite**, so *Işdäňiz açyk bolsun* is **may your appetite be open**. *Ak ýol*, a **white road**, is a road without trouble. In the same pattern you have met *Ertiriňiz haýyrly bolsun*, good morning, and *Agşamyňyz haýyrly bolsun*, good evening.

To one friend, change *-ňYz* to *-ň*: *Ýoluň ak bolsun!*, *Doglan günüň gutly bolsun!*, *Gijäň rahat bolsun!* The words take the endings you know, with their usual changes: *toý* → *toýuňyz* (rounding), *gije* → *gijäňiz* (*e* becomes *ä*), *ömür* → *ömrüňiz* (the second vowel drops, like *burun* → *burnum*).

The answer to a wish is a thank-you: *Sag boluň!*, or *Sag bol!* to a friend. Several wishes often come together in a card or a toast: *Doglan günüňiz gutly bolsun! Ömrüňiz uzak, işiňiz rowaç bolsun!*

lines.en: Hello, Merjen! Congratulations on your celebration!

lines.tk: Sag bol, Maral! Hoş geldiň! Içeri geç.
lines.en: Thank you, Maral! Welcome! Come in.
May the young couple be happy!
Thank you! Sit down, let me bring some food.

blocks.title: Bread and wishes
blocks.text: At a *toý* ([A1 unit 9](a1-u09-culture)) guests arrive with wishes on their lips, and hosts answer with food. Wishes are not small talk in Turkmen: they are said in full, and said again on every new occasion.

blocks.title: Wish the right thing
blocks.text: *gutly bolsun* is for an occasion, a day or an event: a birthday, a holiday, a wedding. To wish a person success, use *Işiňiz rowaç bolsun*; to wish them a good journey, *Ýoluňyz ak bolsun*.

sections.title: OK? It won't do: bolýar, bolmaz

blocks.text: You have used *Bolýar* since [A1 unit 1](a1-u01) for **OK, all right**. It is the present of *bolmak*, literally **it is becoming, it works**. As a question it asks whether something suits the other person, and its negatives turn a plan down.

blocks.caption: Agreeing, asking and refusing
head: Turkmen
Meaning
Use
rows: Is that OK? Does that suit you?
That's not possible. It doesn't work.
refusing politely, or saying something can't be done

blocks.text: *Bolmaz* is the negative of the general present of [A2 unit 4](a2-u04): **it won't be, it won't do**. It is strong: a firm no to something you won't allow. The old saying of [A1 unit 12](a1-u12-culture) uses it: *Gury sözden palaw bolmaz*, you don't get pilaf out of empty words. For a plan that simply doesn't suit you, *Bolmaýar* is softer; give the reason, and offer another time.

items.en: Let's meet at five, is that OK?
Tomorrow doesn't work, I'm at work.
No, that won't do! Don't go out at night.

lines.en: Let's go to the market on Saturday, OK?

lines.tk: Şenbe bolmaýar, meniň işim bar. Ýekşenbe bolýarmy?
lines.en: Saturday doesn't work, I have work. Is Sunday OK?

blocks.title: Asking permission
blocks.text: To ask whether you may do something, you have two ways now: the set phrase of [A2 unit 5](a2-u05), *Girsem bolýarmy?*, and the optative question, *Gireýinmi?*, shall I come in? Both are polite.

summary: **Let me, I'll, shall I?**: stem + `-AýYn`: *geleýin*, *okaýyn*, *Kömek edeýinmi?*
**Let's**: stem + `-AlY` for two people (*Gel, gideli!*), `-AlYň` for a group (*Geliň, başlalyň!*); *Gidelimi?*, shall we go?
A final *e* becomes *ä* and the *t*-verbs voice their *t*: *işläýin*, *gideli*.
**Let him, let them**: stem + `-sYn`, `-sYnlAr`: *gelsin*, *otursynlar*; negative *gelmesin*; question *gelsinmi?*
Wishes: noun + **your** + adjective + *bolsun*: *Toýuňyz gutly bolsun!*, *Ýoluňyz ak bolsun!*, *Işdäňiz açyk bolsun!* Answer *Sag boluň!*
*Bolýar* (OK), *Bolýarmy?* (is that OK?), *Bolmaýar* (that doesn't work), *Bolmaz!* (that won't do!).
